extracted.intended_audience: taxpayers, tax practitioners, employers, payroll/tip-reporting program administrators, and public commenters on proposed IRS regulations
extracted.subtask_short: IRS proposed rule on qualified tips
extracted.subtask_description: Notice of proposed rulemaking that defines the term "qualified tips" for the new section 224 tax deduction, identifies occupations that "customarily and regularly" received tips on or before Dec. 31, 2024, and explains related limits and requirements for claiming the deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Qualified Tips (Section 224(d)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Qualified tips" are cash tips received by an individual in an occupation that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024, as provided by the Secretary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed regulations would define "qualified tips" consistent with section 224(d) and subject to the other limitations and requirements in section 224 and the proposed regulations (e.g., voluntariness, SSTB exclusion, other Secretary-established requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Cash Tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Cash tips include tips received from customers that are paid in cash or charged and, in the case of an employee, tips received under any tip-sharing arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically includes cash, check, credit card, debit card, gift card, tangible or intangible tokens readily exchangeable for fixed amount in cash (e.g., casino chips), and electronic/mobile payments denominated in cash. Excludes items paid in any medium other than cash or charge (e.g., event tickets, meals, services, or other assets not exchangeable for a fixed amount in cash such as most digital assets). Definitions align with IRS guidance for FICA and withholding (§§31.3121(a)(12)-1 and 31.3401(a)(16)-1, Notice 2023-13, Rev. Rul. 2012-18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Payments Must Be Voluntary
rubrics_metrics.description: A payment is a qualified tip only if it is paid voluntarily without any consequence in the event of nonpayment, is not the subject of negotiation, and is determined by the payor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with Revenue Ruling 2012-18 factors used to distinguish tips from service charges: (1) payment free from compulsion; (2) customer has unrestricted right to determine amount; (3) payment not subject to negotiation or dictated by employer policy; (4) customer generally has right to determine who receives payment. Example: an automatically added 18% charge for a large party was a service charge, not a tip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service Charges and Mandatory Amounts Not Qualified (unless optional to customer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Service charges, automatic gratuities, and other mandatory amounts automatically added to a customer's bill by the vendor/establishment are not qualified tips unless the customer is expressly provided an option to disregard or modify it without consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed regulation clarifies that mandatory or employer-dictated charges generally fail the voluntariness test and therefore are treated as service charges rather than qualified tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specified Service Trade or Business (SSTB) Exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts received in the course of a trade or business that is a specified service trade or business (as defined in section 199A(d)(2)) are not qualified tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed regulations apply the SSTB definition in section 199A(d)(2) and Treasury regulation §1.199A-5(b); they also provide that tips received by an employee working for an SSTB employer are not qualified tips regardless of whether the owner may claim a §199A deduction. The Treasury/IRS request comments on the application and possible refinement of §1.199A-5(b) definitions for section 224 purposes and provide examples illustrating the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Employees of SSTB Employers
rubrics_metrics.description: If an employee receives tips while performing services for an employer whose trade or business is an SSTB, those tips are not qualified tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule applies irrespective of whether the trade or business owner is eligible for a §199A deduction (for example, it applies even if employer is a corporation). Examples will be provided in the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: TRDA/GITCA Voluntary Tip Reporting Program Participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Tips reported pursuant to a Tip Rate Determination Agreement (TRDA) or Model Gaming Employee Tip Reporting Agreement (GITCA) count as qualified tips if the participating employee is otherwise eligible for the section 224 deduction and reports tips using the tip rates established under the agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employees participating in TRDA or GITCA receive tip examination protection for years their agreements are in effect; participating employees may also report additional qualified tips to the IRS on Form 4137.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion for Tips from Illegal or Prohibited Activities and Payor-Recipient Ownership/Employment Relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts received for services the performance of which is a felony or misdemeanor under applicable law, amounts received for prostitution services and pornographic activity, and payments where the tip recipient has an ownership interest in or is employed by the payor are not qualified tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These limits are intended to prevent reclassification of income as qualified tips and to prevent abuse of the deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-or-Business Limitation for Non-Employee Trade or Business (Section 224(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: For qualified tips received in the course of a trade or business (other than performing services as an employee), the deduction is taken into account only to the extent that the gross income from that trade or business exceeds deductions allocable to that trade or business for the taxable year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed regulations restate the statutory limit and clarify that the qualified tips deduction itself is not taken into account as a deduction associated with the trade or business when applying the limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Security Number Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: No deduction is allowed under section 224 unless the taxpayer includes on the tax return for the taxable year the Social Security number (SSN) of the individual who received the tips (within the meaning of section 24(h)(7)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed regulations clarify which SSN(s) must be included (only the tip recipient's SSN is required unless both spouses have qualified tips being claimed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Married Filing Joint Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the taxpayer is married, section 224 applies only if the taxpayer and the taxpayer's spouse file a joint return for the taxable year; the deduction is not available for married taxpayers who file separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations clarify the joint-filing requirement and SSN requirements for married taxpayers claiming the deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dollar Limitation and Phase-Out (Section 224(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The deduction is limited to an amount not to exceed $25,000 in a taxable year and is further limited based on a taxpayer's modified adjusted gross income (MAGI); the deduction phases out for taxpayers with MAGI over $150,000 ($300,000 for joint filers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed regulations clarify that the total amount of qualified tips deductible on a return per calendar year is $25,000 regardless of filing status, after which the amount is subject to the MAGI-based phase-out described in section 224(b)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and Termination Dates
rubrics_metrics.description: The section applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, and no deduction is allowed for any taxable year beginning after December 31, 2028.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed regulations restate the statutory applicability and termination dates in sections 224(h) and (g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupations That 'Customarily and Regularly' Received Tips — General Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An occupation is considered to have customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024 if individuals in that occupation received cash tips more often than occasionally during a calendar year ending on or before December 31, 2024.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treasury/IRS looked to dictionary definitions (Oxford English Dictionary) and FLSA guidance. DOL regulation characterizes 'customarily and regularly' as a frequency greater than occasional but which may be less than constant (29 CFR 531.57). Courts and DOL guidance consider extent of customer interaction and other contextual factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupation Inclusion Methodology — Data Sources and Thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Treasury/IRS drafted the proposed occupation list using a review of 2023 Forms W-2, Forms 4137, corresponding Forms 1040 occupation entries, GITCA and other IRS tip reporting program data, survey data (Panel Study of Income Dynamics), and legislative history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occupations were identified based on the percentage of wage earners who reported a given occupation in tax return data and also reported at least $100 in annual tipped income. Where IRS tax data under‑included or did not capture occupations (e.g., independent contractors), the Treasury/IRS supplemented with GITCA, PSID survey data, and the House Budget Committee list. The agencies acknowledge data limitations and made adjustments accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data Screening Rules and Sample Restrictions for Occupation Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: To limit misattribution and improve linkage between reported occupation and tips, the Treasury/IRS limited the main tax return analysis to taxpayers with only one job: taxpayers who submitted one Form W-2 with their Form 1040, did not file a Schedule C or Schedule F, and reported no active income from a partnership or S corporation on Schedule E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This screening reduces ambiguities from multiple-occupation reporting, but the agencies note remaining limitations (typographical variations, multiple occupations in one entry) and possible under- or over-inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for Under- and Over-Inclusion in Occupation Identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and adjust for under-inclusion (e.g., rideshare drivers and other contractors not issuing Form W-2 or Form 4137) and over-inclusion (variations in how taxpayers write occupations) when constructing the occupations list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treasury/IRS supplemented tax return data with GITCA data, survey data, and legislative sources; they also reviewed SOC codes and made occupation-level judgments to avoid including nonsubstantive or mixed SOC categories that would erroneously include non-tipped subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of Occupations Participating in Tip-Sharing Arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Occupations that may not involve direct customer interaction but participate in tip-sharing arrangements (such as tip pools or tip-outs) may be considered occupations that customarily and regularly received tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because section 224(d)(3) includes tips received under tip-sharing arrangements, Treasury/IRS included occupations like dishwashers where tax data showed sufficient reported tips and where tip-sharing arrangements are common. The proposed list therefore covers both direct-customer and tip-shared recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and Mapping of SOC Codes with Caution
rubrics_metrics.description: When mapping Treasury Tipped Occupation Codes to 2018 SOC codes, recognize that some SOC codes cover heterogeneous job types (some of which may not customarily receive tips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agencies explicitly note examples (e.g., 'Animal Caretakers' can include pet caretakers who customarily receive tips and zookeepers who do not) and avoid mechanically including entire SOC categories when subgroups differ in tip practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive Reliance on FLSA and DOL Guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: In interpreting 'customarily and regularly,' the agencies considered FLSA text, legislative history, DOL regulations and guidance, and relevant court decisions addressing frequency and customer interaction requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agencies discuss FLSA's $30/month tipped-employee threshold, DOL's definition that frequency must be greater than occasional but may be less than constant, and case law requiring at least more-than-de-minimis customer interaction for certain tip-pool contexts.
